correctness.rationale: The claim is a genuinely exhaustive finite theorem. I independently reconstructed the standard four-candidate Dodgson and Young scores over all \(24^3=13824\) labeled three-voter profiles, without treating the saved verifier log as proof. Dodgson was computed by exhaustive upward moves of the focal candidate in each ballot (moves among other candidates cannot improve its pairwise margins), and Young by exhaustive nonempty voter-subset deletion with weak Condorcet target. The independent census reproduced exactly 1008 divergent profiles, the histogram \(12288,528,144,576,288\), and strict \(D(P)\subsetneq Y(P)\) in every divergent case. The package verifier additionally double-computes each score and canonicalizes all divergent profiles, yielding seven candidate/voter-relabeling classes of orbit size 144. The one-voter boundary is immediate, and the three-candidate lower candidate boundary is supplied by prior literature.
risks: The theorem is deliberately limited to complete strict rankings and standard weak-Young at four candidates with one or three voters; it does not classify even electorates or larger candidate sets.

value.rationale: Dodgson and Young are classical Condorcet extensions whose exact agreement at three candidates is a known structural boundary. A complete classification of the very first divergence layer is therefore mathematically motivated: it gives the exact incidence, direction of set refinement, winner-set-size strata, and all symmetry types rather than a single witness. This is a natural complete finite classification under the stated value standard.
risks: The result is a first-layer finite theorem and does not extrapolate a frequency law for larger elections.

limitations: Complete strict preferences; standard Dodgson and standard weak-Young only.
Exact only for four candidates with one or three voters.
Originality is best-of-knowledge; weakly indexed finite-election computations remain a residual risk.
